title: MLP gain on J-space directions
takeaway: Across the workspace layer range, MLP blocks amplify directions aligned with the J-space roughly ten times more than random directions, while ordinary neuron output directions are not amplified at all. Among SAE features, amplification rises monotonically with J-lens kurtosis, so the more a direction lies in the J-space, the more strongly the next MLP boosts it.
walkthrough:
The item is a two-panel line chart, and it is the paper's first structural test of [[j-space-broadcast]]: whether the model's weights are built to spread [[j-space]] content down through the layers, rather than that spreading being an accident of particular inputs.

Both panels share the same axes. The horizontal axis is the source layer $\ell$, the depth at which a candidate direction is defined. The vertical axis is [[mlp-gain]]: a unit direction $v$ at layer $\ell$ is fed to the [[mlp-block]] at layer $\ell+1$, and the norm of the block's output is recorded. That norm is divided by the median output norm over isotropic random directions, so a random direction scores 1 by construction. Each curve plots the median gain over 2,000 unit directions from one population. The paper flags the metric as a first-pass approximation, since in natural settings the gain can depend on what else is in the [[residual-stream]] alongside $v$.

The left panel compares two populations. One is the [[j-lens-vector]] population at layer $\ell$ — the directions the [[jacobian-lens]] associates with vocabulary tokens. The other is the output-weight directions of layer-$\ell$ MLP neurons, the directions ordinary neurons write into the stream. The J-lens curve sits near 1 before the workspace onset (around layer 38 in this model), climbs to roughly $10	imes$ through the [[workspace-layers]], and falls again near the output. The neuron curve stays near 1 throughout. The next layer's MLP treats a neuron's own output as unremarkable, and treats a J-lens direction as something to amplify.

The right panel runs the same measurement on [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions, split into six equal strata of 2,000 by their [[lens-kurtosis]] percentile — top 1%, 1–5%, 5–10%, 10–20%, 20–50%, and bottom 50%. Gain orders monotonically with kurtosis: the top-1% stratum is amplified most, and the bottom half stays near baseline. In the early workspace layers the top stratum's gain exceeds the J-lens vectors' own, which the paper reads as a sign that the lens only partially captures the true workspace directions. A companion weight-level analysis ([[neuron-connectivity]]) corroborates the picture.

terms.definition: The horizontal axis: the depth at which each candidate unit direction is defined. The gain is always measured one layer later, at the MLP block of layer ℓ+1.

The vertical axis: the output norm of the layer-(ℓ+1) MLP block applied to a unit direction, divided by the median output norm over isotropic random directions. A value of 1 means the direction is amplified no more than noise.
The feed-forward component of a transformer layer, acting at a single token position; here it is treated as one nonlinear function whose amplification of a direction is measured.
The left panel's first population: one direction per vocabulary token per layer, each encoding the model's disposition to say that token. Their collection defines the J-space.

The left panel's comparison population: the directions that layer-ℓ MLP neurons write into the residual stream. They serve as a control of equally 'real' model directions that are not J-space-aligned.
The normalizing baseline: unit vectors drawn uniformly at random in residual-stream space. The gain scale is defined so their median gain is exactly 1.
The right panel's populations: the write-directions of sparse autoencoder features, an unsupervised dictionary of the model's linear features, used as an independent source of candidate directions.

The right panel's legend: SAE features are ranked by how sharply peaked their J-lens projection is over the vocabulary, then split into six equal samples — top 1%, 1–5%, 5–10%, 10–20%, 20–50%, bottom 50%. High κ means the direction lies in the J-space.
The summary statistic per curve point: the median gain over the 2,000 directions in that population, chosen over the mean to resist outliers.
The depth, about a third of the way through the model, where the J-space begins to carry workspace-like content; in the figure it is where the J-lens gain curve starts to rise from 1.

numbers.meaning: The baseline gain of isotropic random directions, and thus of any direction the MLP treats as noise. It equals 1 by construction, because every gain is divided by the random-direction median. Neuron output-weight directions and the bottom-50% SAE stratum sit near this value at all depths.

The approximate peak gain of J-lens vectors within the workspace layer range: the next MLP block's output on a J-lens direction is roughly ten times larger than on a random direction. The curve rises to this level after the workspace onset and falls again in the final layers.
The number of unit directions sampled per population (and per SAE stratum) at each source layer; each plotted point is the median over these.

The number of equal-sized SAE strata in the right panel, cut at J-lens kurtosis percentiles: top 1%, 1–5%, 5–10%, 10–20%, 20–50%, bottom 50%. Equal sizes make the strata directly comparable; gain orders monotonically across them.
The layer of the MLP block whose gain is measured, one past the source layer ℓ — the first block that could read a direction just written at layer ℓ.
The workspace layer range the paper identifies elsewhere (section 4.1) for this model; the elevated-gain region in the figure tracks this range, near 1 before ~L38 and declining toward the output.
